highlights.text: Ibn Fāris derives ص-ب-ر (ṣ-b-r) from three distinct roots
Al-ṣabr means to hold or confine.
al-ṣabīr: a guarantor or surety, so named because he "endures" (yaṣbiru) the liability.
in al-Aʿshā's line "…that man was not created of stone."
another line of al-Aʿshā, "just before dawn, the sounds of the ṣibār,"
Ibn Fāris notes the Prophet forbade killing any animal this way (ṣabr).
a single core idea: strength or firmness in a thing
ṣidq (truthfulness) — the opposite of lying (kadhib).
ṣadaqa — what a person gives away as charity from himself and his wealth
the mutaṣaddiq is the giver, as in Qur'an 12:88, "and give charity to us"
A line of verse is cited ending "...to a far-off land of few friends (aṣādiq)."
Core sense — to keep company.
الصَّاحِب (al-ṣāḥib) is "the companion, the one who keeps company."
Ibn Sīda cites Q 53:2, (ما ضَلَّ صاحِبُكم وما غَوَى) "Your companion has not strayed nor erred,"
Ibn Sīda reads Q 21:43, (ولا هم منّا يُصْحَبون), as "nor shall they be protected from Us,"
اصطحب / تصاحب: two men became mutual companions.
قضيب مُصْحِب: a rod still in its bark (with a verse of Kuthayyir ʿAzza).
The chest (ṣadr) — of a human and of other things; plural ṣudūr.
but rather the hearts that are within the breasts (al-ṣudūr) grow blind.
ṣadara ʿan al-māʾ ("he departed from the water")
core sense is a color — specifically redness (ḥumra)
ṣubḥ (dawn) is so named for its redness, as is the miṣbāḥ (lamp) for its glow
Al-ṣabāḥ is \"the light of day.\"
yawm al-ṣabāḥ: the day of a raid (attested in a line of al-Aʿshā about morning battle-dust).
\"more lying than the morning-drinking captive\"
a single idea: being clear and free of any admixture.
Ibn Fāris applies this to Muḥammad as صِفْوَةُ اللَّه — God's chosen elect (khiyra) and muṣṭafā from among His creation
smooth, bare stone, so called because it is clear of clay and sand.
with a verse on the smooth rock slipping underfoot
a violent striking together with an intense sound
the thunderbolt, i.e. the violent stroke that accompanies thunder.
"to be struck down / to die,"
**something spread out flat, and breadth/extent**
**صَحِيفة (ṣaḥīfa)** — belonging to the same root-category, the flat surface *written upon*
**صِحَاف (ṣiḥāf)** — on the authority of al-Shaybānī
He cites al-Buʿayth: every man of the tribe of Kulayb has a "face-skin" more abject
carrying two linked ideas: **rising/elevation** and **hardship**
ṣaʿūd is the up-gradient, the opposite of ḥadūr (the down-gradient); the verb is ṣaʿida / yaṣʿadu.
He cites Q 74:17, "I shall burden him with a ṣaʿūd (steep ascent),"
Some hold it is the face of the earth.
illustrated by al-Aʿshā: "If you ask after me — many a questioner has asked eagerly about al-Aʿshā, wherever he set off."
He quotes the Prophet: "Beware of sitting in the roads, except one who renders their due."
Al-Zajjāj held it is the face of the earth and the place, whether or not dust lies on it, and claimed the lexicographers agree ṣaʿīd is not turāb (dust/soil)
one consistent idea running through it: **breadth / a wide flat side**
Ibn Fāris explains this idiom — turning away from someone's wrongdoing — as belonging to the same root-sense
He cites al-Nābigha, whose line describes cleaving doubled-weave Salūqī mail and striking sparks — "the fire of al-ḥubāḥib" — off the broad stones.
having six distinct root-senses: (1) a colour, (2) emptiness, (3) a metal of the earth, (4) a sound, (5) a season/time, (6) a plant.
ṣufra is "yellowness."
citing a verse in which a poet's horses and riding-camels are called ṣufr, "their young ones like raisins."
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-d-f as two separate bases
"We shall requite those who turn away (yaṣdifūna) from Our signs."
the side or flank of a mountain
the ones watching for their turn, the ṣawādif.
core idea is a splitting or parting open in something
Ibn Fāris cites Q 86:12, "and the earth possessing the ṣadʿ."
"so declare openly what you are commanded."
تَصَدَّعَ الْقَوْمُ, the people dispersed / split apart.
**Core sense: yearning / inclining, especially with youthful passion**
ṣibyah, aṣbiyah, uṣaybiyah (diminutive plural), ṣibyān — all mean "young children."
"ṣabawtu ilayhi" = I yearned toward him
Several verses are cited describing droplets of frost or dew rolling down a surface "like strung pearls" (including one by Ibn Muqbil)
a verse by al-Hudhalī praises a blow struck with "every sharp sword possessing a ṣabiyy and a gleam."
one core meaning: to colour or dye something with some colour.
sabaghtuhu asbughuhu - "I dyed it / I dye it."
Some say it means God's fitra - the innate constitution/nature He gave His creation.
Others say it means anything at all by which a person draws near to God
al-Sabi'un - the Qur'anic community name.
Both Qur'anic occurrences of the term are cited: al-Hajj 22:17 ("the Sabi'in and the Christians") and al-Baqarah 2:62 ("the Christians and the Sabi'in").

highlights.text: al-ṣafd means a fetter or shackle (equivalent to al-ghull)
Its plural al-aṣfād means "fetters" (aqyād).
a man named Maʿbad led away bound in a ṣifād
the ḥadīth "When Ramaḍān begins, the devils are shackled (ṣuffidat al-shayāṭīn)"
words scatter across unrelated meanings — no single underlying idea ties them together.
"Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping (taṣdiya)."
The verb taṣaddā (as in taṣaddā li-l-shayʾ) means to lift oneself up and watch something intently
A poet uses it describing a ruined, abandoned dwelling: its echo has gone silent, its traces are worn away
Core sense — the finger.
Iṣbaʿ = "finger," singular of aṣābiʿ ("fingers").
Ibn Fāris quotes the poet al-Rāʿī describing such a shepherd: frail-looking, with a thin staff and veins showing from age
First — a way of standing.
Second — a receptacle.
a horse standing on three legs with the fourth raised
illustrated with a line of poetry about sharing a waterskin in turn
A hadith of al-Barāʾ describes the Companions standing behind the Prophet ṣufūnan (in this attentive posture).
al-qāʿ = smooth, bare ground; al-ṣafṣaf = even, level ground (al-mustawī).
if hurled against it, would be flattened — "turned level" (ʿāda ṣafṣafā).
One consistent, regular root: a tilt/inclination in something.
al-taṣʿīr — turning one's cheek away from looking at someone, out of self-conceit
illustrated with a line of poetry by al-Musayyab
Hadith citation: "there is none among them but aṣʿar or abtar" — glossed as: none but the conceited, or the lowly/disgraced.
one idea, turning away and turning aside
al-ṣadd is turning away; ṣadda, yaṣuddu is inclining toward one of two sides.
al-ṣadīd is blood mixed with pus; aṣadda al-jurḥ means the wound produced it.
one root meaning: evenness in a thing
al-ṣaff is a row.
The people iṣṭaffū or taṣāffū when they line up together.
He cites the verse: "The meat-cooks kept on, some bringing to doneness strips of roast meat, or a hastened pot-dish."
one root meaning, "the pouring out of a thing"
**Pouring.** ṣababtu l-māʾa aṣubbuhu ṣabban: "I poured out the water".
al-Shammākh's verse about a people "after whom I have had life only in its last drops".
it is said of him (God bless him and his family and grant him peace) that when he walked it was as though he were going down a slope (ṣabab)
